sources.title: G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment
sources.authority_note: Peer-reviewed EMNLP paper in ACL Anthology; introduces criteria-driven LLM evaluation with a form-filling output and reports evaluator bias analysis.

sources.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
sources.authority_note: Original benchmark paper from the LMSYS/UC Berkeley research team; empirically studies agreement and position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases in LLM judges.

sources.title: JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 Core and Validation Specifications
sources.authority_note: Official JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 Core specification; section 10.3.2.3 defines additionalProperties behavior for object properties.

sources.title: JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 Validation Specification
sources.authority_note: Official JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 Validation specification; sections 6.1.1 and 6.5.3 define type and required validation assertions.

claims.claim: A judge prompt should state the evaluation task and explicit criteria, then request a constrained form-like verdict rather than an unconstrained quality impression.
claims.source_locator: ACL Anthology paper, abstract and Sections 2-3: criteria prompt, generated evaluation steps, and form-filling evaluator output.
claims.support: G-Eval describes feeding task introduction and evaluation criteria to an LLM and formatting the evaluator output as a form.
claims.scope: Supports the lesson’s bounded rubric and one-verdict response design for a binary regression criterion.
claims.limitations: G-Eval primarily evaluates summarization/dialogue quality and does not establish that any particular binary rubric is valid for this course’s regression.

claims.claim: LLM judges can agree substantially with human preferences while still exhibiting systematic biases, including position, verbosity, and self-enhancement effects; therefore a judge prediction is an auditable proxy, not ground truth.
claims.source_locator: MT-Bench paper abstract and Sections 4-5; G-Eval paper abstract and Section 4 bias analysis.
claims.support: The papers report human agreement alongside documented judge biases, including preference for outputs from the judge’s own model family in G-Eval.
claims.scope: Justifies inspecting disagreements and excluding unrelated qualities from the rubric.
claims.limitations: Bias magnitude depends on model, prompt, task, and comparison protocol; these papers do not predict the behavior of the offline fixture.

claims.claim: A structured response contract can require named fields and reject missing or extra fields, making malformed judge output fail validation before it becomes prediction data.
claims.source_locator: JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 Core, Section 10.3.2.3 (additionalProperties); Validation specification, Sections 6.1.1 (type) and 6.5.3 (required).
claims.support: The Core specification defines additionalProperties behavior for names not matched by properties or patternProperties; the Validation specification defines required and type assertions.
claims.scope: Supports validating case_id, binary verdict, and non-empty reason in cached responses.
claims.limitations: JSON Schema alone does not enforce uniqueness or cross-record exact ID coverage; those require explicit application checks.

claims.claim: Predictions must be joined to reference cases by stable case_id with exactly one response per case; row order is not an adequate identity contract.
claims.source_locator: Application-level invariant derived from the plan’s CP-L02-03-A observable check; JSON Schema source establishes field-level contract but not relational coverage.
claims.support: The source supports validating the case_id field’s presence/type; exact uniqueness, unknown-ID rejection, and coverage are explicit pipeline checks.
claims.scope: Supports the lesson’s one-to-one alignment and preservation of human_label.
claims.limitations: This is a course engineering inference, not a claim that the cited standard specifies joins.

claims.claim: Replaying cached judge responses makes the parsing, alignment, persistence, and disagreement-inspection pipeline reproducible offline, but it does not measure live-provider variance or current model behavior.
claims.source_locator: Inference from the plan’s offline_replay contract, contrasted with the papers’ live-model experimental protocols.
claims.support: The cited studies evaluate particular model/prompt runs; replaying stored responses necessarily fixes those responses and omits new provider calls.
claims.scope: Supports the explicit limitation learners must state for the offline build-along.
claims.limitations: The papers do not evaluate this exact cache design; the reproducibility statement is a pipeline-level inference.

evidence_gaps: No primary source was needed or used for EP-03 confusion-matrix, precision, or recall formulas; those concepts are explicitly out of EP-02 scope.
The sources do not establish universal guarantees for binary judge validity, exact-ID coverage, or cache reproducibility; those remain explicit course engineering invariants and limitations.
